schools.summary: Henry takes Shiggaion for a 'wandering song' or a 'charming song' David sang cheerfully though basely abused, and floats both that Cush covertly names Saul the Cushite and, more likely, a kinsman named Cush.
Clarke derives Shiggaion from shagah, to wander (with Bishop Horsley, a 'wandering ode' or improviso), and reads Cush as 'a name of disguise' for Saul the son of Kish.

Calvin flatly rejects the disguised-Saul theory (David names Saul openly elsewhere) and makes Cush a real Benjamite kinsman; Gill and Calvin stress the present, unbroken tense of 'in thee do I trust.'
Keil and Delitzsch make Cush an actual Benjamite of the persecution and note the deliberate 'concerning the words'; Ellicott renders the trust-clause 'in thee have I taken refuge.'
Augustine reads the title spiritually — Chusi as 'silence,' a 'veil of mysteries' lifted once the reader passes over to Christ.

debates.question: Who is Cush the Benjamite named in the title?

sides.position: a covert or disguised name for Saul himself, the son of Kish
a real Benjamite, one of Saul's kinsmen, distinct from the king
a wandering song (from shagah, to wander), perhaps unpremeditated
a musical term — a kind of tune, melody, or setting

outliers.note: Reads the whole title allegorically and typologically — Chusi interpreted 'silence,' the names lifted as a 'veil of mysteries' pointing past the historical David to Christ.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the shift from plural to singular and the lion as a reminiscence of David's shepherd days (1 Sam. 17:37; Ps. 3:7), with the LXX/Vulg/Syriac 'snatch away'; Keil and Delitzsch tie 'this' to the Benjamite's slanders and contrast poetry with prose.
Gill names the lion Saul — royal, powerful, wrathful — citing Paul's 'lion' (2 Tim. 4:17) and Peter's roaring lion (1 Pet. 5:8).
Clarke presses the figure to Saul, king over the land as the lion over the forest, from whose irresistible power none could deliver.
Gill: 'this' needs no naming — the public charge that David lay in wait for Saul; notes the Targum's 'if I made this song with an evil intention.'
Clarke recalls the charge of affecting the kingdom and meets it with an indignant self-imprecation; Wesley glosses the 'iniquity in my hands' as deeds Cush falsely laid to his charge.
Ellicott binds the verse to the two sparings of Saul (1 Sam. 24:11; 26:18); Keil and Delitzsch again set the poetry beside David's plain prose protest.
Spurgeon: David twice spared Saul (cave and sleeping camp) and can appeal to heaven with a clear conscience, yet the imprecation is most solemn and not to be trifled with.
Gill reads 'him at peace with me' of Saul before the breach, and notes Jarchi's 'if I rewarded him evil for evil' — true rather of Christ the antitype.
Clarke recalls the cave and the cut skirt, David's heart smiting him for the indignity to the Lord's anointed; Wesley glosses 'I have delivered' of when it was in his power to destroy Saul.
Ellicott reads 'so far from returning evil for good, I have returned good for evil,' but suspects textual corruption (Ewald's dropped clauses, supported by LXX/Vulg), and cites Milton's rendering.

outliers.note: Suspects the verse corrupt on metrical grounds — reports Ewald's conjecture that two clauses have dropped out, with LXX and Vulgate support, yielding 'injured my enemy without cause.'

schools.summary: Gill: a plain condition — if the charge could be proved, let Saul pursue, apprehend, and take his life.
Clarke: 'if I have been guilty... let the worst evils fall upon me.'

Ellicott mines the Hebrew — 'let an enemy,' 'persecute' as 'burn,' 'tread' of potter/horses/herd (Isa. 41:25; Ezek. 26:11), 'honour' as the soul (Ps. 22:15; 16:9; 57:8) — and reads Selah as a musical direction.
Spurgeon sees the customary pause heightening the oath's solemnity, and draws the lesson that a true heart's simple word is as binding as an oath.
Gill guards against ascribing local motion to the infinite God: 'arise' is spoken after the manner of men, God coming forth in power and displeasure.

Henry has David plead the enemies' wrath as ground for God's, noting 'rage' is plural — the furies of many foes; Spurgeon feels the daring of bidding the Lord 'awake,' whose seeming sleep is the patience of longsuffering.

Ellicott hears abrupt ejaculations of an excited mind, prefers 'against the rage,' records LXX/Vulg 'in the ends of' (Jerome: 'make an end of my enemies') and the Syriac, and arranges two imperatives.
Wesley: 'lift up thyself' = glorify thyself above them; the 'commanded' judgment is the sentence declared by the prophet Samuel.
Gill takes the congregation for the twelve tribes surrounding the altar with songs of deliverance, rejecting the 'hostile encompassing' reading of some Jewish commentators.
Clarke pictures the anxious faithful and prays God to mount the tribunal so all may see the innocent and guilty; Wesley has the people come from all parts to worship at the tribunal set on high.

Ellicott renders 'let the communities of peoples be gathered round thee' and sees arraigned nations favouring a community reading; Keil and Delitzsch call this 'the key to all Psalms which contain prayers against one's enemies,' aimed at wickedness not persons.

debates.question: What is the 'congregation' compassing God, and what is the 'return on high'?

sides.position: David's own nation gathering to worship as God mounts the tribunal — the psalm an individual's plea
the assembled peoples of the earth arraigned at judgment — the psalm the community's voice

schools.summary: Gill: God is Judge of all the earth who pleads his own cause; David asks to be judged by his righteousness and the sincerity of his heart, while owning only Christ can attest uprightness in all things.
Clarke: 'judge me' = let my innocence be brought to light and my just dealing made clear as noonday.
Spurgeon sees David, hand on an honest heart, pleading his integrity in the matter between himself and Saul as the court opens.

Ellicott reports Jerome ('David could not say this; it belongs to the sinless Saviour') and the 'ideal Israel' view, but himself refers the plea to David's innocence of the calumny, comparing Job's protestations.

debates.question: How can the psalmist ask to be judged 'according to my righteousness'?

sides.position: the plea belongs properly to Christ alone, the sinless one
it is the ideal Israel/community standing before the tribunal
David's relative innocence of the specific calumny, not sinless perfection

themes: judge me according to my righteousness
a clear conscience in the cause

schools.summary: Gill reaches past particular foes to the end of all wickedness in the new-Jerusalem state, and notes 'let wickedness now consume the wicked'; the petition voices hatred of sin.

Henry reads a double desire — the destruction of sin and the perpetuity of righteousness; Spurgeon calls it the universal longing of the elect and marvels at the search that tries the hearts and reins.
Clarke keeps it concrete: 'the wickedness of the wicked' is Saul's conduct, 'establish the just' a prayer that David's uprightness be seen.
Ellicott renders 'let him stand erect' and addresses God directly as 'thou trier of hearts and reins,' the verb used of assaying metals (Ps. 12:6; Prov. 17:3).

themes: let wickedness come to an end

schools.summary: Gill weighs 'my shield is in/of/with God,' of God himself, or of Christ the shield of faith who pleads his people's cause.

Henry opens his long meditation on two pillars — God's favour to the sincere and his respect for justice (name a strong tower, Prov. 18:10); Spurgeon hears triumph, the slandered one hymning his Lord as providence brushes off the flung filth.
Clarke: 'I now leave my cause in the hands of my Judge,' unafraid, knowing God saves the upright in heart.
Ellicott fixes 'my shield is upon God' (cf. Ps. 62:7) and cites Milton; Keil and Delitzsch add the balancing warning of daily threatenings to the ungodly (Isa. 66:14).
Gill takes 'judgeth the righteous' of God protecting those made righteous by Christ, allowing 'God is a righteous Judge.'
Henry: the wicked are children of wrath, God angry with them every day, his anger new every morning, even in their prosperity and prayers.

Clarke mounts a long textual case that the Hebrew reads 'not angry every day' (the el/al crux, 'with the wicked' borrowed from the Chaldee, backed by the versions); Wesley: angry even when providence seems to favour them.
Ellicott reports but rejects the emendation, keeping 'God is a righteous judge, and God avengeth every day.'

debates.question: Does the verse read 'God is angry with the wicked every day' or 'God is not angry every day'?

sides.position: 'not angry every day' — reading 'not' for 'God,' with the ancient versions; God is longsuffering

schools.summary: Gill: not God but the wicked man must turn; unless converted he stands under the whetted blade; LXX/Vulg/Arabic/Ethiopic read 'if ye turn not.'
Clarke joins the clause to the previous verse and reads the two together; Wesley: God will hasten and speedily execute his judgments.

Ellicott calls it doubly idiomatic, 'surely he will again whet his sword,' with 'bent' literally 'trodden'; Keil and Delitzsch make God the subject who whets the sword against the impenitent (Deut. 32:41), rejecting 'again whet.'
Henry finds mercy in the menace — the gracious proviso 'if he turn not' means the destruction may still be prevented by conversion.

debates.question: Does the opening mean 'if he turn not' (the sinner's repentance) or 'surely he will again' (whet)?

sides.position: 'if he turn not' — the impenitent sinner is the subject who must repent
'surely, he will again whet his sword' — an idiom of repetition, not of repentance

schools.summary: Gill: the instruments of death are the weapons of God's indignation, issuing in the first death and the second.
Wesley marks persecutors as the fairest marks of divine wrath; Clarke alone reads the verse as a specific prophecy of Saul's death by Philistine arrows and his own sword.
Henry lingers over the variety of weapons — sword at hand, bow and arrows at a distance (Job 20:24) — made ready yet not hastily used, God giving warning and space to repent.
Ellicott renders 'against the persecutors' as 'for those burning' — fiery arrows tipped with flame (cf. Eph. 6:16), Milton's 'arrows barb'd with fire.'

outliers.note: Reads the verse as a specific prophecy of the tragical death of Saul, wounded by Philistine arrows and falling on his own sword — where the others take a general truth of judgment.

schools.summary: Gill: the man is so big with iniquity, as a woman with child, that he is in pain till he brings it forth in act.
Clarke sees the pitch of Saul's malevolence, all his expectations blasted; Wesley reads the deep design and restless endeavour that will not rest till accomplished.
Ellicott: God's judgments are not arbitrary but follow sin as its consequence (Job 15:35); Keil and Delitzsch note man reaps what he sows, and the singular order of travail before pregnancy.

Henry describes head and heart conceiving and travailing, yet bringing forth only falsehood, wind, stubble, and death; Spurgeon's three strokes — travail, unhallowed conception, and the progeny of the father of lies.
Gill: he dug the pit large and capacious to answer his purpose, only to tumble into it himself.
Clarke pictures the covered pit disguised with reeds, and quotes Bishop Horne on the equity of the guilty suffering the punishment they meant for the innocent.
Spurgeon dwells on the stooping labour of secret entrapment and the digger fallen in his own trench; Henry draws the rule that mischief against God's people is made to return on their own heads.
Ellicott compares Abigail's sling (1 Sam. 25:29) and Eusebius's application to Constantine's defeat of Maxentius, whose bridge of boats prepared his own destruction.

themes: made a pit and digged it

schools.summary: Gill: whatever the wicked man devised against others falls back on himself, a just judgment from heaven.
Henry: they prepare destruction for themselves by preparing themselves for destruction, their violence recoiling by the righteous hand of God.
Clarke glosses 'pate' by the Hebrew kodkod, the crown or scalp, perhaps a blow on the head, even (had it been known) scalping.
Ellicott notes 'pate' retained from Coverdale and common in Shakespeare's age, recalling Abigail's blessing (1 Sam. 25:29) and the engine that ruins its builder.

themes: mischief returns on his own head

schools.summary: Gill: praise 'according to his righteousness' in vindicating the innocent and punishing the wicked, as Moses sang when Pharaoh was drowned.
Clarke celebrates justice and mercy together, unfolds 'the name of the LORD most high' as Jehovah's perfections, and cites an old Scoto-English psalter's paraphrase.
Henry reads the fit end — glory to God for protection and for just vengeance; Spurgeon's joyful contrast, the jewel on a black foil, the harp restrung and mounting to adoring praise.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the reader to the concluding note of thanksgiving toward which the closing strophe had moved.

themes: the name of the LORD most high
